questions.stem: In the context of physiological control systems, the feedforward mechanism primarily involves:

options.label: A
options.text: Preemptive responses initiated by efferent signals after detecting a change in the controlled variable.

options.label: B
options.text: Sequential activation of afferent pathways to stimulate motor neurons and induce a rapid response to a predictable stimulus.

options.label: C
options.text: Proactive adjustments by the body that anticipate and prepare for an expected change in the environment or a controlled variable.

options.label: D
options.text: Retrograde signaling facilitating a prompt feedback loop to counteract any deviation from the set point in physiological parameters.

questions.answerText: Proactive adjustments by the body that anticipate and prepare for an expected change in the environment or a controlled variable.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Proactive adjustments by the body that anticipate and prepare for an expected change in the environment or a controlled variable.

 

The feedforward mechanism in physiological control systems is designed to anticipate changes and initiate appropriate responses before the actual deviation occurs. Unlike feedback control, which relies on detecting an error before correcting it, feedforward control acts in advance based on prediction and anticipation.

 

Examples of feedforward mechanisms include:

 

  • Core temperature regulation: The body anticipates temperature fluctuations and adjusts accordingly.
  • Increase in heart rate before exercise: Even before physical activity starts, the body increases heart rate in preparation.
  • Cephalic phase of digestion: The anticipation of food triggers gastric acid secretion before the food reaches the stomach.

 

These examples highlight that feedforward control does not require immediate feedback or a stimulus but instead proactively prepares for an expected event.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Preemptive responses initiated by efferent signals after detecting a change in the controlled variable: This describes feedback control rather than feedforward control. In feedback control, the system detects a change first and then initiates a correction. In contrast, feedforward control acts before any measurable change occurs.

 

Option B. Sequential activation of afferent pathways to stimulate motor neurons and induce a rapid response to a predictable stimulus: This statement aligns more with reflex arcs or reactive responses rather than anticipatory feedforward mechanisms. Feedforward control does not depend on afferent pathways and motor neuron activation but rather on preemptive adjustments based on expected conditions.

 

Option D. Retrograde signaling facilitating a prompt feedback loop to counteract any deviation from the set point in physiological parameters: This describes a feedback loop rather than feedforward control. Feedback control mechanisms detect deviations from a set point and initiate corrective actions, while feedforward control anticipates changes before they happen.

 

Educational Objective: 

 

Feedforward control is a physiological mechanism that anticipates and prepares for a change before it occurs, ensuring preemptive adjustments rather than reactive corrections.

questions.stem: A physiological control system exhibits a gain of 0.6. If a change in the input stimulus leads to a corresponding 12% change in the controlled variable, what is the magnitude of the alteration in the input stimulus that would result in a 30% change in the controlled variable?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) 1.25 units

 

Given a gain of 0.6, which represents the ratio of the change in the controlled variable to the change in the input stimulus, and a 12% change in the controlled variable due to a change in the input stimulus, we can calculate the alteration in the input stimulus required for a 30% change in the controlled variable using the formula: Change in input stimulus = (Desired change in controlled variable / Gain). Therefore, (30% / 0.6) = 1.25 units of change in the input stimulus would result in a 30% change in the controlled variable. 

 

Gain = Correction / error

 

Error = Correction / gain

questions.stem: Which of the following accurately describes a specific function of phospholipids within the cell membrane?

options.label: A
options.text: Phospholipids regulate membrane fluidity and flexibility.

options.label: B
options.text: Phospholipids serve as energy storage molecules within the lipid bilayer, aiding in cellular metabolism.

options.label: C
options.text: Phospholipids act as signaling molecules, transmitting extracellular signals across the membrane surface.

options.label: D
options.text: Phospholipids form the selective permeability barrier of the cell membrane, allowing controlled passage of substances in and out of the cell.

questions.answerText: Phospholipids form the selective permeability barrier of the cell membrane, allowing controlled passage of substances in and out of the cell.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Phospholipids form the selective permeability barrier of the cell membrane, allowing controlled passage of substances in and out of the cell.

 

Phospholipids are amphipathic molecules, meaning they have both hydrophilic (water-attracting) heads and hydrophobic (water-repelling) tails. This dual nature enables them to form the lipid bilayer of the cell membrane, which acts as a selective permeability barrier. This barrier regulates which substances can enter or exit the cell, allowing lipid-soluble molecules to pass through while restricting water-soluble molecules.

 

The permeability of the cell membrane is primarily determined by the hydrophobic tails of phospholipids, which prevent the free movement of polar molecules and ions. Instead, transport proteins embedded in the membrane help regulate the passage of these substances.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Phospholipids regulate membrane fluidity and flexibility: This is incorrect because cholesterol, not phospholipids, is the key molecule responsible for maintaining membrane fluidity and flexibility. Cholesterol fits between the phospholipid molecules in the bilayer, preventing excessive rigidity at low temperatures and excessive fluidity at high temperatures.

 

Option B. Phospholipids serve as energy storage molecules within the lipid bilayer, aiding in cellular metabolism: This is incorrect because phospholipids are structural components of the membrane, not energy storage molecules. The body primarily stores energy in the form of triglycerides in adipose tissue, not in the phospholipid bilayer.

 

Option C. Phospholipids act as signaling molecules, transmitting extracellular signals across the membrane surface: This is incorrect because cellular signaling is mainly facilitated by proteins, such as receptor proteins and G-protein-coupled receptors, rather than phospholipids. While some phospholipids (like phosphatidylinositol derivatives) play a secondary role in signal transduction, the primary function of phospholipids is forming the membrane structure.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Phospholipids primarily function as structural components of the cell membrane, forming a selective permeability barrier. This property allows lipid-soluble substances to cross while restricting water-soluble molecules, thereby maintaining cellular integrity and function.

questions.stem: In a patient presenting with severe muscle weakness and an inability to breathe properly, the underlying pathology involves a genetic mutation affecting a protein crucial for the function of microfilaments. Which of the following proteins is most likely to be implicated in this condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Actin

 

Actin is a crucial component of microfilaments, which are part of the cytoskeleton and play a fundamental role in muscle contraction, cell movement, and intracellular transport. In muscle cells, actin exists in two forms: G-actin (globular actin) and F-actin (filamentous actin). When G-actin polymerizes, it forms F-actin, which interacts with myosin to generate the force required for muscle contraction.

 

A mutation in the actin gene (ACTA1) can lead to severe muscle disorders such as nemaline myopathy, characterized by muscle weakness, respiratory difficulty, and impaired movement. Since the diaphragm is a muscle crucial for respiration, actin mutations can result in breathing difficulties, as seen in this patient.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Myosin: Myosin is a motor protein that interacts with actin to facilitate muscle contraction. However, myosin is not a microfilament; it is a thick filament in the muscle sarcomere. While mutations in myosin can cause muscle disorders, they do not directly affect microfilament function.

 

Option C. Tropomyosin: Tropomyosin is a regulatory protein that binds to actin filaments and helps control muscle contraction by blocking or allowing myosin binding sites on actin. However, tropomyosin itself is not a microfilament and does not play a primary role in actin filament formation or structural integrity.

 

Option D. Nebulin: Nebulin is a large protein associated with actin filaments in muscle cells, primarily functioning as a stabilizer for actin filaments. While mutations in nebulin (NEB gene) can also cause muscle weakness, nebulin does not form the actual microfilament structure like actin does.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Actin is the primary protein forming microfilaments, which are essential for muscle contraction and cellular structure. Mutations in actin-related genes can lead to severe muscle disorders, including nemaline myopathy, affecting movement and breathing.

questions.stem: In a patient diagnosed with familial dilated cardiomyopathy (FDC), genetic studies reveal mutations in genes encoding proteins crucial for maintaining cardiac adherens junctions. Which specific protein alteration is most likely to contribute to the pathogenesis of FDC?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) β-catenin

 

Adherens junctions play a crucial role in maintaining structural integrity and mechanical stability between cardiac muscle cells, particularly in the intercalated discs. These junctions allow the heart to function as a coordinated syncytium, ensuring force transmission during contraction.

 

β-catenin is a key component of adherens junctions, linking cadherin proteins to the actin cytoskeleton. In familial dilated cardiomyopathy (FDC), mutations in β-catenin or cadherin-related genes disrupt the mechanical and electrical coupling between cardiomyocytes, leading to weakened cardiac muscle, progressive dilation, and impaired contractility. This structural dysfunction contributes to heart failure, a hallmark of FDC.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. JAM-A (Junctional Adhesion Molecule A): JAM-A is primarily involved in tight junctions, not adherens junctions. Tight junctions function mainly as barriers regulating paracellular permeability, whereas adherens junctions provide mechanical stability between cells. Since the question specifically mentions adherens junctions, JAM-A is not the correct answer.

 

Option B. Desmin: Desmin is an intermediate filament protein found in skeletal and cardiac muscle cells. It functions as a cytoskeletal marker, providing structural support to the muscle fibers. While desminopathies can cause myopathies and cardiomyopathies, desmin is not part of adherens junctions, making it an incorrect choice.

 

Option D. Vimentin: Vimentin is also an intermediate filament protein, but it is mainly expressed in mesenchymal cells, including fibroblasts and endothelial cells. It plays a role in maintaining cell integrity and migration but is not directly involved in adherens junctions of cardiac muscle cells.

 

Educational Objective:

 

β-catenin is a key protein in adherens junctions, linking cadherins to the actin cytoskeleton. Mutations in β-catenin-related genes can weaken cardiac muscle integrity, leading to familial dilated cardiomyopathy (FDC) and progressive heart failure due to impaired mechanical coupling between cardiomyocytes.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic kidney disease presents with elevated serum potassium levels. Despite treatment, the patient remains at risk of hyperkalemia due to impaired renal excretion. The compartment of body fluid Which is primarily responsible for potassium regulation, what percentage does it represent as compared to Extracellular fluid?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Approximately 200% 

 

Potassium is primarily regulated within the intracellular fluid (ICF) compartment. The total body water (TBW) is divided into two major compartments:

 

  • Intracellular Fluid (ICF) – approximately 40% of body weight
  • Extracellular Fluid (ECF) – approximately 20% of body weight

 

This distribution follows the 60-40-20 rule, where 60% of body weight is total body water, 40% is ICF, and 20% is ECF. Since ICF contains nearly 98% of total body potassium, it plays a crucial role in potassium homeostasis.

 

When comparing ICF to ECF in terms of potassium regulation, we find that:

 

ICF=2×ECF

 

Thus, the ICF compartment is approximately 200% of the ECF compartment in relation to potassium content, making option A the correct answer.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Potassium homeostasis is primarily maintained by the intracellular fluid (ICF) compartment, which contains nearly 98% of the body's potassium. The ICF volume is approximately 200% of the ECF volume, highlighting the critical role of intracellular potassium in maintaining membrane potential, nerve function, and muscle contraction.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old male with a history of congestive heart failure presents to the emergency department with complaints of progressive shortness of breath and fatigue. His medications include furosemide, enalapril, and spironolactone. Laboratory tests show a serum sodium concentration of 125 mmol/L and a serum potassium concentration of 5.0 mmol/L. Using the Darrow-Yannet diagram, which of the following best represents his fluid and electrolyte status (Dotted line representing normal condition)?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D.

 

 

This patient has hyponatremia due to diuretic therapy (furosemide and spironolactone) in the setting of congestive heart failure (CHF). CHF leads to extracellular fluid (ECF) expansion due to sodium and water retention, but the use of diuretics promotes free water loss, leading to hyponatremia.

 

To correctly interpret the Darrow-Yannet diagram, let’s break down the fluid shifts:

 

1. Understanding the Fluid Status:

 

  • Hyponatremia (↓ Na⁺ concentration) → ↓ ECF osmolarity.
  • CHF with diuretics → Loss of both Na⁺ and water, leading to ECF volume contraction.
  • Hypo-osmolar state causes water to shift from ECF → ICF, leading to ICF expansion.

 

2. Darrow-Yannet Diagram Interpretation:

 

  • ECF volume decreases (due to diuretic-induced fluid loss).
  • ICF volume increases (due to osmotic water shift into the cells in response to low sodium).
  • Osmolarity decreases overall (hyponatremia results in a hypo-osmolar state).

 

Matching the Diagram to the Condition:

 

  • Option D correctly represents these changes:
    • ECF volume contraction (smaller ECF space).
    • ICF expansion (water shift into the cells).
    • Decreased osmolarity (shift downward).

 

Thus, Option D is the correct representation of the patient’s fluid and electrolyte status.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Incorrect: This diagram shows an increase in osmolarity, which would be seen in hypernatremia, not hyponatremia.

 

Option B. Incorrect: This shows ECF volume expansion, which is not expected with diuretic use.

 

Option C. Incorrect: This represents hyperosmolar dehydration (e.g., diabetes insipidus), not the hypo-osmolar state seen in hyponatremia.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Diuretic-induced hyponatremia in CHF leads to decreased ECF volume, increased ICF volume, and reduced osmolarity. The correct Darrow-Yannet diagram shows ECF contraction, ICF expansion, and a hypo-osmolar state.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old patient is diagnosed with syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) due to a small cell lung carcinoma. This patient presents with hyponatremia and concentrated urine despite normal kidney function. Which of the following changes in body fluid compartments is most likely associated with this condition?

options.label: A
options.text: Expansion of intravascular fluid and decreased intracellular fluid

options.label: B
options.text: Expansion of interstitial fluid and decreased intravascular fluid

options.label: C
options.text: Expansion of intracellular fluid and decreased interstitial fluid

options.label: D
options.text: Expansion of intravascular fluid and increased intracellular fluid

questions.answerText: Expansion of intravascular fluid and increased intracellular fluid
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Expansion of intravascular fluid (IVF) and increased intracellular fluid 

 

SIADH is characterized by excessive secretion of antidiuretic hormone (ADH), also called vasopressin, leading to increased water retention and hyponatremia.

 

  1. Mechanism of SIADH:
    • ADH increases water reabsorption by acting on V2 receptors in the renal collecting ducts, increasing the insertion of aquaporin-2 channels in the nephron.
    • This causes excessive free water retention, leading to expansion of extracellular fluid (ECF), including the intravascular compartment (plasma volume).
    • However, because only water is retained (without proportional solute retention), the plasma osmolarity decreases, leading to dilutional hyponatremia.
    • The osmotic imbalance between the extracellular and intracellular compartments causes water to shift into the intracellular compartment, leading to intracellular expansion as well.
  2. Fluid Compartment Changes in SIADH:
    • Expansion of intravascular fluid (ECF/plasma volume increases) → Due to water retention from increased ADH.
    • Expansion of intracellular fluid (ICF increases) → Because hypo-osmolar ECF drives water into cells.

 

Thus, both ECF (intravascular) and ICF expand, making option D the correct answer.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Expansion of intravascular fluid and decreased intracellular fluid: While ECF expands, intracellular fluid does not decrease. Instead, water shifts into the ICF due to reduced ECF osmolarity, increasing ICF volume.

 

Option B. Expansion of interstitial fluid and decreased intravascular fluid: The entire ECF (including plasma) expands, not just the interstitial fluid. Also, intravascular fluid does not decrease in SIADH.

 

Option C. Expansion of intracellular fluid and decreased interstitial fluid: While ICF increases, interstitial fluid also increases as part of the ECF expansion. There is no selective decrease in interstitial fluid.

 

Educational Objective:

 

SIADH leads to increased ADH secretion, causing free water retention, expansion of both ECF and ICF, and dilutional hyponatremia. The osmotic gradient shifts water from ECF to ICF, resulting in intracellular swelling.

questions.stem: In a patient with glucose-galactose malabsorption, an inherited disorder leading to impaired absorption of glucose and galactose in the small intestine, which transporter mechanism is primarily affected?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) SGLT1 symporter

 

Glucose-galactose malabsorption is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by a mutation in the SLC5A1 gene, which encodes the Sodium-Glucose Linked Transporter 1 (SGLT1).

 

  1. Function of SGLT1:
    • SGLT1 is responsible for the active transport of glucose and galactose from the intestinal lumen into enterocytes using a sodium (Na⁺) gradient.
    • This symporter (co-transporter) relies on Na⁺-K⁺ ATPase, which creates a sodium gradient that drives glucose and galactose uptake against their concentration gradients.
  2. Pathophysiology in Glucose-Galactose Malabsorption:
    • Due to a mutation in SGLT1, glucose and galactose cannot be absorbed from the intestinal lumen.
    • This leads to osmotic diarrhea, dehydration, and severe metabolic disturbances (e.g., hyponatremia).
    • However, fructose absorption remains normal, as it is transported via GLUT5, which functions through facilitated diffusion (not active transport).

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. GLUT1 transporter:

 

  • GLUT1 is a facilitated glucose transporter found in the blood-brain barrier and erythrocytes.
  • It does not play a role in intestinal glucose and galactose absorption, making it irrelevant to this condition.

 

Option C. GLUT4 transporter:

 

  • GLUT4 is an insulin-dependent glucose transporter found in muscle and adipose tissue.
  • It is involved in glucose uptake in response to insulin but does not mediate glucose absorption in the intestine.

 

Option D. GLUT2 transporter:

 

  • GLUT2 facilitates basolateral transport of glucose, galactose, and fructose from enterocytes into the bloodstream, not the initial absorption from the intestinal lumen.
  • While GLUT2 is important for intestinal glucose transport, the primary defect in glucose-galactose malabsorption lies in SGLT1, which prevents glucose from even entering enterocytes in the first place.

 

Educational Objective:

 

SGLT1 is the key transporter responsible for glucose and galactose absorption in the small intestine. A mutation in SGLT1 (SLC5A1 gene) leads to glucose-galactose malabsorption, which presents with severe osmotic diarrhea, dehydration, and metabolic imbalances. Fructose absorption remains intact due to the GLUT5 transporter, which operates via facilitated diffusion.

questions.stem: In a patient with malignant hyperthermia triggered by anesthesia, which of the following alterations in the process of excitation-contraction (EC) coupling is primarily responsible for the rapid onset of muscle rigidity and hyperthermia?

options.label: A
options.text: Dysregulation of L-type calcium channels in the sarcolemma

options.label: B
options.text: Overactivity of calcium channels in the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR)

options.label: C
options.text: Impaired release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction

options.label: D
options.text: Reduced activity of voltage-gated sodium channels in the muscle membrane

questions.answerText: Overactivity of calcium channels in the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR)
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Overactivity of calcium channels in the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR)

 

Malignant hyperthermia (MH) is a life-threatening genetic disorder of skeletal muscle that occurs due to exposure to volatile anesthetics (e.g., halothane, sevoflurane) or depolarizing muscle relaxants (e.g., succinylcholine). It results from a mutation in the RYR1 gene, which encodes the ryanodine receptor (RYR1), the calcium release channel of the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR).

 

  1. Pathophysiology of Malignant Hyperthermia:
    • Normally, excitation-contraction (EC) coupling involves the activation of L-type voltage-gated calcium channels (DHPR) in the T-tubule, which then mechanically activate RYR1 receptors in the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) to release calcium (Ca²⁺).
    • In MH, defective RYR1 channels remain abnormally open, leading to excessive and sustained calcium release into the cytoplasm of muscle cells.
    • This leads to:
      • Persistent muscle contraction (rigidity)
      • Increased ATP consumption (due to excessive calcium cycling by SERCA pumps trying to reabsorb Ca²⁺)
      • Excessive heat production (hyperthermia) due to ATP hydrolysis
      • Lactic acidosis and rhabdomyolysis due to metabolic stress
  2. Key Features of Malignant Hyperthermia:
    • Muscle rigidity
    • Hyperthermia (rapid increase in body temperature)
    • Metabolic acidosis and hypercapnia (increased CO₂ levels due to high metabolic rate)
    • Tachycardia and arrhythmias due to hyperkalemia from muscle breakdown
    • Elevated creatine kinase (CK) and myoglobinuria (due to rhabdomyolysis)
  3. Treatment:
    • Dantrolene is the antidote for MH. It works by blocking RYR1 channels, preventing further calcium release and restoring muscle relaxation.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Dysregulation of L-type calcium channels in the sarcolemma (DHPR):

 

  • L-type calcium channels (Dihydropyridine receptors, DHPR) are located on the sarcolemma/T-tubule membrane, but they do not release calcium into the cytoplasm in skeletal muscle.
  • Instead, they activate the RYR1 receptors on the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which then release calcium.
  • The defect in MH is not in the DHPR channel, but in the RYR1 receptor itself.

 

Option C. Impaired release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction:

 

  • Acetylcholine (ACh) release is involved in nerve-to-muscle signaling at the neuromuscular junction, but it is not the primary defect in malignant hyperthermia.
  • Disorders like myasthenia gravis or Lambert-Eaton syndrome involve ACh transmission defects, but they do not cause hyperthermia and excessive muscle contraction.

 

Option D. Reduced activity of voltage-gated sodium channels in the muscle membrane:

 

  • Voltage-gated sodium channels (Nav1.4) in muscle are important for action potential generation, but they are not responsible for calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
  • A mutation in sodium channels (e.g., SCN4A mutation) can cause periodic paralysis, not malignant hyperthermia.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Malignant hyperthermia results from overactivation of ryanodine receptors (RYR1) in the sarcoplasmic reticulum, leading to excessive calcium release, muscle rigidity, ATP depletion, and hyperthermia. The primary treatment is Dantrolene, which directly inhibits RYR1-mediated calcium release.

questions.stemHtml: Preload is the stretching of the cardiac muscle fibres at the end of diastole, just before contraction. It is due to an increase in ventricular pressure caused by the filling of blood during diastole. An image is provided below that further supplements the findings stated above. These are expressions of?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Frank starling’s law

 

Frank-Starling’s Law states that the stroke volume (SV) of the heart increases in response to an increase in the volume of blood filling the heart (preload), when all other factors remain constant. This means that greater ventricular preload (end-diastolic volume) leads to increased myocardial fiber stretching, resulting in stronger contractions and higher stroke volume.

 

The graph in the image:

 

  • X-axis: Ventricular preload
  • Y-axis: Stroke volume
  • The ascending portion (preload-dependent zone): Stroke volume increases with increasing preload (responsive patients, SVV > 10%).
  • The plateau phase (preload-independent zone): Stroke volume no longer increases significantly with increased preload (non-responsive patients, SVV < 10%).

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Vascular hyalinosis: Refers to hyaline deposition in blood vessels, commonly seen in hypertension and diabetes. It does not relate to preload and stroke volume relationships.

 

Option C. Vascular capacitance: Refers to the ability of blood vessels to expand and store blood, mainly in veins. While veins influence preload, Frank-Starling’s Law specifically explains the heart’s response to preload, not vascular capacitance.

 

Option D. Vascular resistance: Describes opposition to blood flow within vessels, mainly regulated by arterioles. While vascular resistance affects afterload, it does not directly describe preload-stroke volume relationships.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Frank-Starling’s Law explains how increasing ventricular filling (preload) enhances myocardial contraction and stroke volume, up to a certain limit. This principle is crucial in understanding heart function, fluid responsiveness, and circulatory dynamics.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old male severs an artery in a motorcycle accident. A bystander applies a tourniquet to stop the bleeding. When the paramedics arrived, the blood pressure of the injured man was only slightly hypotensive and his pupils were reactive. The greatest percentage of the redistributed blood volume came from which of the following?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Venules and veins 

 

  • Venules and veins have the greatest percentage of the redistributed blood volume. It means the largest portion of blood at rest is in systemic veins and venules. 
  • The greatest percentage of the redistributed blood volume in this case would come from the veins, specifically the venules and veins distal to the site of the tourniquet. 
  • This is because the veins are more compliant than arteries and arterioles, and can hold a larger volume of blood. 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Heart: Acts as a pump, not a blood reservoir.

 

Option B. Aorta: Functions as a conduit, not a storage vessel.

 

Option C. Arteries and Arterioles: Regulate distribution, but do not store blood for redistribution.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Veins and venules are capacitance vessels that store blood. In hemorrhage, venoconstriction shifts blood into circulation, helping maintain cardiac output and blood pressure.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man visits his physician because he finds it difficult to hold his hand steady when painting. Examination reveals a resting tremor and rigidity. The symptoms are relieved by a single dose of levodopa. This patient’s neurological signs are most likely related to a lesion within which of the following?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) The substantia nigra 

 

The patient presents with resting tremors, rigidity, and responsiveness to levodopa, which are classic features of Parkinson’s disease. Parkinson’s disease results from dopaminergic neuron degeneration in the substantia nigra pars compacta, which disrupts the nigrostriatal pathway.

 

The "BTR" mnemonic—Bradykinesia, Tremor (resting), and Rigidity—is useful for recognizing Parkinsonism. These symptoms arise due to dopamine depletion in the basal ganglia, leading to excessive inhibition of movement. The classic resting tremor (pill-rolling tremor) occurs at 3–6 Hz and improves with voluntary movement. Other key symptoms include a shuffling gait and postural instability.

 

Levodopa, a precursor of dopamine, temporarily relieves symptoms, confirming dopaminergic dysfunction as the underlying pathology.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. The cerebellum:

 

  • The cerebellum is primarily responsible for coordinating voluntary movements and balance. A lesion here would cause intention tremor, ataxia, or festinating gait (not resting tremor).
  • Parkinson’s tremors are resting tremors, whereas cerebellar lesions cause intention tremors, which worsen as the patient reaches for an object.

 

Option C. The premotor area:

 

  • The premotor cortex, located in the frontal lobe, is involved in planning and coordinating voluntary movements.
  • Damage here leads to difficulty initiating movements (apraxia) but does not cause resting tremors or rigidity.

 

Option D. The caudate nucleus and putamen (Striatum):

 

  • The caudate nucleus and putamen are components of the basal ganglia but are not the primary site of degeneration in Parkinson’s disease.
  • Damage here can lead to chorea (involuntary, irregular, dance-like movements, seen in Huntington’s disease) or athetosis (slow, writhing movements, associated with lentiform nucleus damage).

 

Educational Objective:

 

Parkinson’s disease is caused by degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, leading to bradykinesia, resting tremor, and rigidity. It is treated with levodopa, which temporarily restores dopamine levels

questions.stem: Physical examination of a 41-year-old narcotic abuser reveals an early systolic murmur. The physician also notes a 7 cm distance between the height of the blood in his right internal jugular vein and the sternal angle (normal = 3 cm). Which of the following conditions is most likely responsible for the physical findings?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Tricuspid regurgitation 

 

The key findings in this case are:

 

  1. A 7 cm jugular venous pressure (JVP) elevation (normal is ~3 cm above the sternal angle).
  2. An early systolic murmur.
  3. History of IV drug use (narcotic abuse).

 

Elevated JVP indicates increased right atrial pressure, which is typically seen in conditions affecting the right heart. The most common cause of right atrial pressure elevation in IV drug users is tricuspid regurgitation (TR) due to infective endocarditis from bacterial infection (often Staphylococcus aureus).

 

Mechanism of Tricuspid Regurgitation:

 

  • Tricuspid valve damage leads to backflow of blood into the right atrium during systole, increasing right atrial pressure and thereby elevating JVP.
  • This produces a prominent systolic "V wave" in the JVP waveform and a holosystolic murmur that increases with inspiration (Carvallo’s sign).

 

Since the tricuspid valve is located on the right side of the heart, regurgitation leads to right heart overload, causing venous congestion and an increased JVP.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Mitral stenosis:

 

  • Mitral stenosis is a left-sided heart lesion that increases left atrial pressure, not right atrial pressure.
  • Severe mitral stenosis can cause pulmonary hypertension, which might indirectly increase JVP, but this occurs in advanced cases and is not the primary mechanism here.

 

Option C. Atherosclerosis:

 

  • Atherosclerosis affects arterial circulation, not venous return or JVP.
  • It does not cause systolic murmurs or increased JVP in isolation.

 

Option D. Aortic regurgitation:

 

  • Aortic regurgitation is another left-sided heart condition where blood flows back into the left ventricle during diastole.
  • It is associated with a diastolic murmur, bounding pulses, and a wide pulse pressure rather than elevated JVP or a systolic murmur.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Tricuspid regurgitation, often caused by infective endocarditis in IV drug users, leads to an increased JVP and a holosystolic murmur that intensifies with inspiration. It is characterized by right heart overload and venous congestion.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old female visited her doctor with complaints of pain in her lower back for the last 3 months. While giving her history, she says that she feels excessive fatigue and tiredness and she got a fracture in her left radius 2 months back. Her blood investigations were done and reports showed significant vitamin D deficiency. The doctor prescribed him a vitamin D tablet which will absorb with the help of which component of the cell membrane?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Lipid 

 

Vitamin D is a fat-soluble vitamin, meaning that it is absorbed through the lipid bilayer of the cell membrane without requiring a specific transporter.

 

There are two main types of molecules based on their solubility:

 

  1. Lipid-soluble substances (e.g., steroid hormones, vitamin A, vitamin D, and thyroid hormones)
    • These can cross the cell membrane directly due to their hydrophobic (lipophilic) nature.
    • They bind to intracellular receptors (either cytoplasmic or nuclear receptors) to exert their effects.
  2. Water-soluble substances (e.g., peptide hormones, insulin, growth factors)
    • These cannot cross the lipid bilayer directly and require membrane-bound receptors such as ion channels, protein pumps, or GPCRs.

 

Since Vitamin D is lipid-soluble, it dissolves in lipids and diffuses across the phospholipid bilayer of the cell membrane without needing a protein transporter.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Aquaporins:

 

  • Aquaporins are water channels that allow passive diffusion of water molecules across the cell membrane.
  • Vitamin D is not water-soluble, so it does not require aquaporins for absorption.

 

Option C. Protein pump:

 

  • Protein pumps are active transport mechanisms that move ions and molecules against their concentration gradient (e.g., Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase).
  • Vitamin D does not require active transport; it passively diffuses through the lipid bilayer.

 

Option D. Ion channels:

 

  • Ion channels are protein structures that allow the selective passage of ions (e.g., sodium, calcium, potassium, chloride) across the membrane.
  • Since Vitamin D is not an ion, it does not rely on ion channels for absorption.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Vitamin D is a fat-soluble vitamin that crosses the cell membrane through passive diffusion via the lipid bilayer, without requiring specialized transport proteins or channels.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man visits his doctor because his wife has long complained of his snoring, but recently observed that his breathing stops for a couple of minutes at a time while he is sleeping. He undergoes polysomnography and ventilatory response testing to ascertain the extent and cause of his sleep apnea. The activity of the central chemoreceptors is stimulated by which of the following?

options.label: A
options.text: A decrease in the metabolic rate of the surrounding brain tissue

options.label: B
options.text: A decrease in the PO2 of blood flowing through the brain

options.label: C
options.text: An increase in the PCO2 of blood flowing through the brain

options.label: D
options.text: An increase in the pH of the CSF

questions.answerText: An increase in the PCO2 of blood flowing through the brain
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) An increase in the PCO2 of blood flowing through the brain 

 

The central chemoreceptors, located in the medulla, are primarily responsible for detecting changes in PCO₂ and pH in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).

 

  1. CO₂ is a gas and can cross the blood-brain barrier (BBB).
  2. Once inside the CSF, CO₂ reacts with H₂O to form carbonic acid (H₂CO₃) via the enzyme carbonic anhydrase.
  3. Carbonic acid is unstable and dissociates into H⁺ (hydrogen ions) and HCO₃⁻ (bicarbonate ions).
  4. This increase in H⁺ concentration (acidic pH) stimulates the central chemoreceptors, triggering an increase in respiratory rate to expel CO₂ and restore homeostasis.

 

Thus, an increase in PCO₂ in the blood indirectly lowers the pH in the CSF, which stimulates the central chemoreceptors to drive ventilation.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. A decrease in the metabolic rate of the surrounding brain tissue:

 

  • A lower metabolic rate would reduce CO₂ production, leading to lower stimulation of central chemoreceptors, not higher.
  • This is incorrect because CO₂ buildup (not a decrease) is the main stimulus for central chemoreceptors.

 

Option B. A decrease in the PO₂ of blood flowing through the brain:

 

  • Central chemoreceptors do NOT respond to oxygen levels.
  • Peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid and aortic bodies) respond to hypoxia (low PO₂), not central chemoreceptors.
  • Since O₂ cannot cross the BBB efficiently, changes in blood O₂ do not influence central chemoreceptors directly.

 

Option D. An increase in the pH of the CSF:

 

  • An increase in pH (alkalosis) would decrease respiratory drive, not stimulate it.
  • In contrast, a decrease in CSF pH (acidosis) due to increased CO₂ is what actually stimulates the central chemoreceptors.
  • If the pH were to increase, it would indicate CO₂ washout, reducing the need for ventilation.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Central chemoreceptors, located in the medulla, are stimulated by an increase in CO₂ levels in the blood. CO₂ crosses the blood-brain barrier, reacts with water to form carbonic acid, which dissociates into H⁺ and HCO₃⁻. This increase in H⁺concentration (lower CSF pH) stimulates ventilation to remove excess CO₂.

questions.stem: When capillary and interstitial hydrostatic pressures are 3 mm of Hg and 0 mm of Hg and colloid oncotic pressure of capillaries and interstitium is 25 mm of Hg and 5 mm of Hg, What is the Net filtration pressure?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) 17 mm Hg

 

Net Filtration Pressure = k [(Pc - Pi) - (πc-πi)] 

 

  • Replacing the values we get; 
  • Net Filtration Pressure = (3 — 25) — (0 — 5) 
  • = -17mm Hg 
  • The minus sign indicates that fluid movement is inward into the capillary. 
  • So the answer is 17 mm Hg.

questions.stem: A 53-year-old male is brought to the emergency department with complains of right sided weakness and jargon speech. A CT brain was ordered to rule out haemorrhagic stroke. On neurological examination, there is normal object recognition but loss of comprehension. Which of the following areas is affected?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Superior temporal gyrus

 

The patient presents with jargon speech and loss of comprehension, which are classic signs of Wernicke’s aphasia (sensory aphasia). Wernicke’s area is located in the superior temporal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere (usually the left hemisphere in right-handed individuals).

 

  • Wernicke’s aphasia (fluent aphasia) is characterized by:
    • Fluent but meaningless speech (jargon speech)
    • Poor comprehension
    • Word salad (words strung together without logical meaning)
    • Unaware of their deficit (anosognosia)
    • Intact motor function (speech is produced fluently, but without meaningful content)

 

Since motor speech function is intact, Broca’s area (inferior frontal gyrus) is not affected.

  • The superior temporal gyrus (which houses Wernicke’s area) is responsible for language comprehension. A lesion here leads to loss of comprehension while speech remains fluent but nonsensical.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Inferior frontal gyrus (Broca’s area):

 

  • Broca’s area is responsible for speech production.
  • Damage here causes Broca’s aphasia (expressive aphasia), where the patient understands speech but struggles to produce fluent speech.
  • Since the patient in this case has fluent speech but impaired comprehension, Broca’s area is not affected.

 

Option C. Arcuate fasciculus:

 

  • The arcuate fasciculus is a white matter tract that connects Broca’s and Wernicke’s areas.
  • Damage here causes conduction aphasia, where the patient has intact comprehension and speech production but impaired repetition.
  • Since this patient has comprehension deficits, this is not a case of conduction aphasia.

 

Option D. Both A & B:

 

  • If both Wernicke’s and Broca’s areas were damaged, it would cause global aphasia, where both speech production and comprehension are impaired.
  • This patient has fluent speech with poor comprehension, indicating that only Wernicke’s area is affected.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Wernicke’s aphasia is caused by damage to the superior temporal gyrus in the dominant hemisphere. It leads to fluent but nonsensical speech (jargon speech) with impaired comprehension, while motor speech remains intact.

questions.stem: Mark the incorrect statement about Gating of Protein Channels:

options.label: A
options.text: In the case of voltage gating, the molecular conformation of the gate or its chemical bonds responds to the electrical potential across the cell membrane.

options.label: B
options.text: Some protein channel gates are opened by the binding of a chemical sub- stance (a ligand) with the protein, which causes a conformational or chemical bonding change in the protein molecule that opens or closes the gate.

options.label: C
options.text: Effect of the neurotransmitter acetylcholine on its receptors serves as a voltage-gated ion channel.

options.label: D
options.text: A strong negative charge on the inside of the cell membrane may cause the outside sodium gates to remain tightly closed. Conversely, when the inside of the membrane loses its negative charge, these gates open suddenly and allow sodium to pass inward through the sodium pores.

questions.answerText: Effect of the neurotransmitter acetylcholine on its receptors serves as a voltage-gated ion channel.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Effect of the neurotransmitter acetylcholine on its receptors serves as a voltage-gated ion channel.

 

There are two main types of ion channel gating mechanisms:

 

  1. Voltage-gated channels – Open or close in response to changes in membrane potential.
  2. Ligand-gated channels – Open when a specific molecule (ligand) binds to the channel.

 

Why is Option C Incorrect?

 

  • Acetylcholine (ACh) receptors are ligand-gated, not voltage-gated.
  • When ACh binds to nicotinic receptors, it directly opens ligand-gated cationic channels, allowing Na⁺ and K⁺ ions to flow through.
  • Voltage-gated channels, in contrast, open in response to membrane potential changes, not neurotransmitter binding.
  • The neuromuscular junction (NMJ) is a classic example where ACh binds to ligand-gated channels, leading to membrane depolarization, which then activates voltage-gated Na⁺ channels for further propagation of action potential.

 

Thus, the incorrect statement is that acetylcholine receptors are voltage-gated, when in reality, they are ligand-gated.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. In the case of voltage gating, the molecular conformation of the gate or its chemical bonds responds to the electrical potential across the cell membrane:

 

  • Voltage-gated ion channels open/close due to changes in membrane potential.
  • Example: Voltage-gated Na⁺ and K⁺ channels during action potential conduction.

 

Option B. Some protein channel gates are opened by the binding of a chemical sub- stance (a ligand) with the protein, which causes a conformational or chemical bonding change in the protein molecule that opens or closes the gate:

 

  • Ligand binding causes a conformational change in the channel protein, opening or closing the gate.
  • Example: Acetylcholine-gated Na⁺ channels at the neuromuscular junction.

 

Option D. A strong negative charge on the inside of the cell membrane may cause the outside sodium gates to remain tightly closed. Conversely, when the inside of the membrane loses its negative charge, these gates open suddenly and allow sodium to pass inward through the sodium pores:

 

  • Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels have two gates:
    • Activation gate (M gate) – Located on the extracellular side, opens during depolarization.
    • Inactivation gate (H gate) – Located on the intracellular side, closes during repolarization.
  • At resting membrane potential (-70 mV), the activation gate is closed.
  • As depolarization occurs, inside negativity decreases, leading to activation of Na⁺ channels and Na⁺ influx.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Ligand-gated channels open in response to a neurotransmitter (e.g., acetylcholine-gated Na⁺ channels), while voltage-gated channels open in response to membrane potential changes (e.g., Na⁺ and K⁺ channels in action potentials).

questions.stem: Which of the following statements are incorrect about vasopressin?

options.label: A
options.text: It's a more powerful vasoconstrictor than angiotensin II.

options.label: B
options.text: Concentration of circulating blood vasopressin after severe hemorrhage can increase enough to attenuate reductions in arterial pressure markedly.

options.label: C
options.text: Uses adenylyl cyclase-cAMP as well as phospholipase C system.

options.label: D
options.text: Secreted by paraventricular nucleus of hypothalamus

questions.answerText: Secreted by paraventricular nucleus of hypothalamus
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Secreted by paraventricular nucleus of hypothalamus.

 

  • Vasopressin is primarily synthesized by the supraoptic nucleus of the hypothalamus and then transported to the posterior pituitary for release.
  • While the paraventricular nucleus also produces some vasopressin, its main function is the release of oxytocin and autonomic regulation.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. It's a more powerful vasoconstrictor than angiotensin II:

 

  • Angiotensin II is the most potent vasoconstrictor in the body, but vasopressin (ADH) is also a strong vasoconstrictor, especially in conditions like severe hypotension and hemorrhage.
  • In extreme situations, vasopressin can surpass angiotensin II in vasoconstrictive power.

 

Option B. Concentration of circulating blood vasopressin after severe hemorrhage can increase enough to attenuate reductions in arterial pressure markedly:

 

  • After severe hemorrhage, vasopressin is released in high concentrations to cause vasoconstriction, helping maintain arterial blood pressure.

 

Option C. Uses adenylyl cyclase-cAMP as well as phospholipase C system:

 

  • Vasopressin works via two receptor pathways:
    • V1 receptors → Phospholipase C pathway (IP3/DAG system) → Vasoconstriction
    • V2 receptors → Adenylyl cyclase-cAMP pathway → Insertion of aquaporins in the kidney for water reabsorption
  • Since both pathways are used by vasopressin, this statement is correct.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Vasopressin (ADH) is primarily synthesized by the supraoptic nucleus of the hypothalamus and stored in the posterior pituitary. The paraventricular nucleus mainly produces oxytocin. Vasopressin acts via both the phospholipase C (V1) and cAMP (V2) pathways.

 

  • Paraventricular nucleus secretes oxytocin and supraoptic nucleus secretes vasopressin.

questions.stem: A 55yrs old smoker having difficulty in breathing was diagnosed with pulmonary lung fibrosis has saturation of 89%. The cause of this reduced saturation is defect in which mechanism?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Simple diffusion

 

The primary mechanism for gas exchange (oxygen and carbon dioxide transfer) across the alveolar-capillary membrane is simple diffusion. Oxygen moves from the alveoli into the pulmonary capillaries based on its partial pressure gradient without requiring energy or transport proteins.

 

In pulmonary fibrosis, the alveolar walls become thickened due to excessive collagen deposition and scarring. This increases the diffusion distance for oxygen and impairs gas exchange, leading to reduced oxygen saturation (hypoxemia).

 

Factors affecting oxygen diffusion in pulmonary fibrosis:

 

  1. Thickened alveolar walls → Increased diffusion distance
  2. Reduced lung compliance → Impaired alveolar expansion
  3. V/Q (ventilation/perfusion) mismatch → Inefficient gas exchange

 

Because simple diffusion is the primary mechanism for oxygen transport, its impairment explains the low oxygen saturation (89%) in this patient.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Facilitated diffusion:

 

  • Facilitated diffusion requires a transport protein, but gas exchange does not require proteins.
  • Oxygen crosses the alveolar-capillary barrier via simple diffusion without the aid of carrier proteins.

 

Option C. Primary active transport: 

 

  • Primary active transport requires ATP and moves substances against their concentration gradient (e.g., Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase).
  • Oxygen diffusion is passive and follows its gradient, so it does not require energy.

 

Option D. Secondary active transport:

 

  • Secondary active transport uses energy from ion gradients (e.g., Na⁺/glucose cotransport).
  • Oxygen does not rely on ion gradients or co-transport mechanisms; it diffuses freely across the alveolar membrane.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Gas exchange across the alveolar-capillary membrane occurs via simple diffusion, driven by the partial pressure gradient of oxygen. Pulmonary fibrosis impairs diffusion by thickening the alveolar walls, reducing oxygen transport, and leading to hypoxemia.

questions.stem: In the aftermath of an terrorist attack, humanitarian emergency volunteers handed out isotonic drink solutions containing NaCl and glucose to people with signs of dehydration. These oral rehydration solutions with NaCl and glucose are physiologically more effective than isotonic solutions containing NaCl only. Which of the following is the best explanation?

options.label: A
options.text: Primary active glucose transporter at the basolateral intestinal cell membrane facilitates Na+ and water reabsorption from the gut.

options.label: B
options.text: Oral glucose increases insulin secretion, which then facilitates water reabsorption.

options.label: C
options.text: The addition of glucose makes it more likely for the person to drink.

options.label: D
options.text: The cotransport of glucose and Na+ across the apical membrane of intestinal epithelial cells facilitates Na+ and water absorption from the gut.

questions.answerText: The cotransport of glucose and Na+ across the apical membrane of intestinal epithelial cells facilitates Na+ and water absorption from the gut.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) The cotransport of glucose and Na+ across the apical membrane of intestinal epithelial cells facilitates Na+ and water absorption from the gut.

 

Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS) is highly effective in treating dehydration, especially in cases of diarrhea and shock. This effectiveness is primarily due to the sodium-glucose cotransport system in the small intestine, which enhances sodium and water absorption.

 

  1. Sodium-glucose linked transporter (SGLT-1) is present on the apical membrane of intestinal epithelial cells.
  2. SGLT-1 facilitates the cotransport of Na⁺ and glucose into the intestinal cells, increasing sodium absorption in the gut.
  3. This creates an osmotic gradient, which drives water reabsorption into the bloodstream.
  4. Water follows sodium via osmosis, improving fluid retention and rehydration efficiency.

 

This mechanism is why glucose-containing ORS is more effective than a solution containing NaCl alone.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Primary active glucose transporter at the basolateral intestinal membrane facilitates Na⁺ and water reabsorption from the gut:

 

  • While the basolateral membrane has GLUT-2 (a glucose transporter), this is not the primary mechanism behind ORS effectiveness.
  • The key absorption process occurs at the apical membrane via SGLT-1, which is a secondary active transporter, not a primary active one.

 

Option B. Oral glucose increases insulin secretion, which facilitates water reabsorption:

 

  • Insulin does not regulate intestinal water absorption.
  • While glucose can stimulate insulin release, ORS absorption via SGLT-1 happens independently of insulin.

 

Option C. The addition of glucose makes it more likely for the person to drink: 

 

  • While ORS solutions with glucose taste better, the physiological reason for their effectiveness is the sodium-glucose cotransport mechanism, not just increased fluid intake.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS) is effective because the sodium-glucose cotransporter (SGLT-1) in the small intestine allows Na⁺ and glucose to be absorbed together. This creates an osmotic gradient, drawing water into the bloodstream and improving hydration more efficiently than NaCl-only solutions.

questions.stem: In a patient presenting with a suspected gastrointestinal motility disorder, an endoscopic biopsy reveals alterations of Dense bodies in smooth muscle tissue. Which structural feature found at a specific site within smooth muscle cells is associated with the attachment of actin filaments and contributes to the contractile function. This altered structure is analogous to which structure found in skeletal muscle?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Z line 

 

In smooth muscle cells, dense bodies serve as anchoring sites for actin filaments. These structures play a crucial role in contraction, similar to the Z lines (Z discs) in skeletal muscle.

 

  1. Z Line in Skeletal Muscle (Striated Muscle):
    • In skeletal muscle, actin filaments are anchored at the Z line.
    • The Z line defines the boundary of a sarcomere and is the attachment site for thin filaments (actin).
    • When muscle contracts, actin filaments slide over myosin, bringing Z lines closer together.
  2. Dense Bodies in Smooth Muscle:
    • Smooth muscle lacks a well-organized sarcomere structure like skeletal muscle.
    • Instead of Z lines, dense bodies anchor actin filaments, allowing for contraction.
    • These dense bodies serve the same role as Z lines, providing structural support and transmitting force during contraction.

 

Since dense bodies in smooth muscle are functionally equivalent to Z lines in skeletal muscle, the correct answer is B (Z Line).

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. A Band:

 

  • The A band is the region of the sarcomere containing thick filaments (myosin) in skeletal muscle.
  • It does not serve as an attachment site for actin.

 

Option C. M Line 

 

  • The M line is in the center of the sarcomere and anchors myosin filaments, not actin filaments.
  • It does not correspond to dense bodies in smooth muscle.

 

Option D. H Band (H Zone) 

 

  • The H band is the part of the A band where only thick filaments (myosin) are present.
  • It disappears during contraction, but it has no functional equivalence to dense bodies.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Dense bodies in smooth muscle serve as attachment points for actin filaments, similar to the Z line in skeletal muscle. These structures play a key role in contraction by allowing actin-myosin interactions and force transmission.

questions.stem: From which of the following does the tetanic contraction of a skeletal muscle fiber results from a cumulative increase in the intracellular concentration?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Ca++ 

 

Tetanic contraction occurs when repeated stimulation of a muscle fiber leads to a sustained contraction without relaxation. This results from a cumulative increase in intracellular calcium (Ca²⁺) levels due to high-frequency action potentials.

 

  1. Role of Ca²⁺ in Skeletal Muscle Contraction:
    • Muscle contraction is triggered by the release of Ca²⁺ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) into the cytoplasm.
    • Ca²⁺ binds to troponin, which moves tropomyosin away from actin binding sites, allowing myosin heads to bind and initiate contraction.
    • As action potentials increase in frequency, Ca²⁺ does not fully return to the SR, leading to higher intracellular Ca²⁺ levels and sustained contraction (tetany).
  2. Tetanic Contraction Mechanism:
    • Single action potential → Single twitch
    • Repeated high-frequency action potentials → Increased Ca²⁺ in cytoplasm → Sustained contraction (tetany)
    • The more Ca²⁺ remains in the cytoplasm, the stronger and more prolonged the contraction.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. ATP 

 

  • ATP is necessary for muscle contraction and relaxation but does not cause tetanic contraction.
  • ATP is required for:
    • Myosin head detachment from actin (cross-bridge cycling)
    • Ca²⁺ reuptake into the SR via the SERCA pump
  • However, tetany is caused by sustained Ca²⁺ presence, not ATP levels.

 

Option C. K⁺ (Potassium) 

 

  • K⁺ plays a role in repolarization of the action potential, but it does not directly trigger contraction.
  • While changes in extracellular K⁺ levels can affect muscle excitability, it does not cause tetany.

 

Option D. Na⁺ (Sodium) 

 

  • Na⁺ is crucial for action potential generation, but it does not cause sustained contraction.
  • Sodium influx initiates depolarization, but muscle contraction depends on Ca²⁺ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Tetanic contraction in skeletal muscle occurs due to a cumulative increase in intracellular Ca²⁺, which prevents full relaxation between successive action potentials. This sustained Ca²⁺ elevation maintains actin-myosin cross-bridging, leading to continuous contraction.

questions.stem: Which of the following is incorrect with respect to Resting Membrane Potential in Different Cell Types:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Smooth muscle: −8 to −12 mV

 

The resting membrane potential (RMP) is determined by ion gradients across the cell membrane and the permeability of K⁺, Na⁺, and Cl⁻ channels. Different cell types have different RMP values based on their function and ion channel expression.

 

  • Smooth muscle: −8 to −12 mV 
    • The correct RMP of smooth muscle is around −50 mV, not −8 to −12 mV.
    • −8 to −12 mV is the lowest RMP in the body, seen in red blood cells (RBCs), which lack membrane potential-dependent ion channels.

 

Thus, the incorrect statement is option D, as smooth muscle cells do not have such a low RMP.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Neurons: −60 to −70 mV: Neurons typically have an RMP of −70 mV, maintained by the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase pump and K⁺ leak channels.

 

Option B. Skeletal muscle: −85 to −95 mV: Skeletal muscle cells have a more negative RMP than neurons, around −90 mV, allowing for rapid depolarization during action potential initiation.

 

Option C. Hair cells (cochlea): −15 to −40 mV: The hair cells of the inner ear cochlea have a less negative RMP (−15 to −40 mV) due to continuous K⁺ influx from the endolymph, which is crucial for auditory transduction.

 

Educational Objective:

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is incorrect about the Donnan Effect?

options.label: A
options.text: There are more proteins in plasma than in interstitial fluid, there is a Donnan effect on ion movement across the capillary wall.

options.label: B
options.text: Donnan and Gibbs showed that in the presence of a non-diffusible ion, the diffusible ions distribute themselves so that at equilibrium their concentration ratios are equal.

options.label: C
options.text: Due to more charged proteins in the interstitial fluid, cells don’t absorb water, swell up and burst.

options.label: D
options.text: At equilibrium the distribution of permeant ions across the membrane is asymmetric, an electrical difference exists across the membrane

questions.answerText: Due to more charged proteins in the interstitial fluid, cells don’t absorb water, swell up and burst.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Due to more charged proteins in the interstitial fluid, cells don’t absorb water, swell up and burst

 

The Donnan Effect (Donnan Equilibrium) describes how charged, non-diffusible particles (such as proteins) influence the distribution of diffusible ions across a membrane, leading to an asymmetrical ion distribution and osmotic effects.

 

  1. Plasma proteins (non-diffusible anions) are more concentrated in the plasma than in interstitial fluid.
    • This creates an osmotic pressure (oncotic pressure), which helps retain water in the capillaries and prevents excessive fluid loss into the interstitial space.
    • This is a key factor in maintaining fluid balance in the body.
  2. Why is Option C Incorrect?
    • The statement claims that more charged proteins are in the interstitial fluid, which is incorrect.
    • Plasma, not interstitial fluid, has more proteins.
    • If the interstitial fluid had more proteins, it would draw water out of cells, leading to cell shrinkage (not swelling or bursting).
    • In reality, the low protein content in interstitial fluid prevents excessive water movement into the interstitium, thus preventing edema.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. There are more proteins in plasma than in interstitial fluid, there is a Donnan effect on ion movement across the capillary wall: Plasma proteins (non-diffusible anions) influence the distribution of ions, preventing excessive loss of fluid into the interstitial space.

 

Option B. Donnan and Gibbs showed that in the presence of a non-diffusible ion, the diffusible ions distribute themselves so that at equilibrium their concentration ratios are equal: The Donnan-Gibbs equilibrium states that ions will distribute asymmetrically across a membrane if one type of ion cannot pass through, balancing both osmotic and electrical gradients.

 

Option D. At equilibrium, the distribution of permeant ions is asymmetric, and an electrical difference exists across the membrane:

 

  • Due to the presence of non-diffusible ions (proteins), diffusible ions do not distribute equally, leading to a membrane potential.
  • This asymmetry is essential for cell function, such as in nerve impulses and muscle contraction.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The Donnan Effect explains how non-diffusible anions (e.g., plasma proteins) affect the distribution of diffusible ions and fluid movement. Plasma has more proteins than interstitial fluid, creating oncotic pressure to prevent excessive water loss from capillaries. Interstitial fluid does not have high protein content, so cells do not swell or burst due to water absorption.

questions.stem: A motorcyclist suffered head injury 6 months back and presents with persistent memory deficits following injury. Choose the most appropriately matched option related to memory?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Medial Temporal lobe - Declarative memory 

 

Memory is broadly categorized into two types:

 

  1. Declarative (Explicit) Memory → Requires conscious awareness
    • Subtypes:
      • Episodic Memory (events, personal experiences)
      • Semantic Memory (facts, general knowledge)
    • Key structures:
      • Hippocampus (important for consolidating short-term to long-term memory)
      • Medial temporal lobe (stores and processes declarative memory)
      • Neocortex (long-term storage)
  2. Non-Declarative (Implicit) Memory → Does not require conscious awareness
    • Subtypes:
      • Procedural Memory (skills, habits, motor tasks)
      • Priming (unconscious improvement in recognizing stimuli)
      • Associative Learning (conditioning responses)
      • Non-Associative Learning (reflex pathways)
    • Key structures:
      • Striatum (procedural memory)
      • Cerebellum (motor learning)
      • Amygdala & Cerebellum (associative learning)

 

Why is Option C Correct?

 

  • The medial temporal lobe, including the hippocampus, plays a crucial role in declarative (explicit) memory.
  • It is responsible for episodic memory (personal experiences) and semantic memory (facts).
  • Head injury often affects the medial temporal lobe, leading to persistent memory deficits—especially anterograde amnesia (inability to form new memories).

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Hippocampus and implicit memory:

 

  • Hippocampus is associated with declarative (explicit) memory, not implicit memory.
  • Implicit memory is linked to procedural learning (striatum, cerebellum, amygdala).

 

Option B. Neocortex and associative learning:

 

  • Associative learning (like Pavlovian conditioning) involves the amygdala and cerebellum, not the neocortex.
  • The neocortex is important for long-term storage of declarative memory, but not associative learning.

 

Option D. Angular gyrus - Procedural memory:

 

  • Procedural memory (skills, habits, motor learning) is controlled by the striatum and cerebellum, not the angular gyrus.
  • The angular gyrus is involved in language processing and higher cognitive functions, not procedural memory.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The medial temporal lobe, including the hippocampus, is essential for declarative memory (episodic and semantic). Damage to this region, such as in head injuries, results in memory deficits, particularly anterograde amnesia.

questions.stem: A gardener was accidentally poisoned by a weed killer that inhibits acetylcho-linesterase. Which of the following alterations in neurochemical transmission at brain cholinergic synapses is the most likely result of this poisoning?

options.label: B
options.text: A pileup of choline outside the cholinergic neuron (in the synaptic cleft)

options.label: C
options.text: A pileup of acetylcholine outside the cholinergic neuron (in the synaptic cleft)

questions.answerText: A pileup of acetylcholine outside the cholinergic neuron (in the synaptic cleft)
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) A pileup of acetylcholine outside the cholinergic neuron (in the synaptic cleft)

 

Acetylcholinesterase is an enzyme responsible for breaking down acetylcholine (ACh) in the synaptic cleft into choline and acetate after neurotransmission. If this enzyme is inhibited—such as by certain pesticides or nerve agents—acetylcholine is not degraded effectively. This leads to an accumulation of acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft, causing prolonged activation of cholinergic receptors. The excess neurotransmitter results in overstimulation of the nervous system, leading to symptoms such as muscle twitching, excessive salivation, convulsions, and, in severe cases, respiratory failure due to overstimulation of the diaphragm.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Blockade of cholinergic receptors: Acetylcholinesterase inhibition does not block receptors; rather, it leads to excessive stimulation due to increased acetylcholine availability. Receptors remain functional but are over-activated.

 

Option B. A pileup of choline outside the cholinergic neuron: Normally, acetylcholinesterase breaks acetylcholine into choline and acetate, which are recycled. Since the enzyme is inhibited, acetylcholine is not broken down, meaning choline does not accumulate in the synaptic cleft.

 

Option D. Up-regulation of postsynaptic cholinergic receptors: Persistent receptor activation due to excess acetylcholine typically leads to down-regulation rather than up-regulation. The body decreases receptor numbers when overstimulation occurs, not the opposite.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Acetylcholinesterase inhibition leads to an accumulation of acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft, causing prolonged cholinergic activity, which can result in severe neurological and muscular effects.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old male diagnosed with bronchial asthma since last 10 years. Pulmonary function tests are done to assess lung functions. Which of the following is true:

options.label: B
options.text: VC reduces but FEV1 is normal

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) VC normal but FEV1 reduces

 

Bronchial asthma is an obstructive lung disease characterized by bronchoconstriction, airway inflammation, and mucus production, leading to airflow limitation, particularly during expiration.

 

  • Forced Expiratory Volume in 1 second (FEV1) measures how much air a person can exhale forcefully in one second. In asthma, bronchoconstriction leads to increased airway resistance, reducing FEV1.
  • Vital Capacity (VC), which represents the total amount of air a person can exhale after a deep breath in, generally remains normal in obstructive lung diseases because lung volumes are not primarily affected.
  • FEV1/FVC ratio is reduced because FEV1 decreases significantly, whereas Forced Vital Capacity (FVC) remains normal or only slightly affected.

 

Thus, in asthma, FEV1 is reduced, but VC remains normal, making option A correct.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. VC reduces but FEV1 is normal.

 

  • In asthma, FEV1 is always reduced due to increased airway resistance.
  • VC remains normal unless there is severe lung remodeling or chronic hyperinflation, which is uncommon in early asthma.

 

Option C. FEV1/FVC ratio normal.

 

  • The FEV1/FVC ratio is reduced in asthma. Since FEV1 decreases more than FVC, the ratio is lower than normal (<70% in obstructive lung disease).

 

Option D. Functional Residual Capacity (FRC) reduces.

 

  • FRC is the volume of air remaining in the lungs after a normal exhalation.
  • In asthma, due to air trapping, FRC often increases rather than decreases. Expiration is more affected than inspiration, leading to residual air accumulation.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In obstructive lung diseases like asthma, FEV1 decreases due to airway narrowing, VC remains normal, and FEV1/FVC ratio is reduced due to increased airway resistance.

questions.stemHtml: A 28-year-old woman is diagnosed with myasthenia gravis. She is referred to a pulmonologist for a pulmonary function test. Spirometry reveals that her pulmonary volumes are normal. Based on her spirometry, at which of the following lung volumes will the expiratory muscles have the greatest force:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) B 

 

To determine the point where expiratory muscles generate the greatest force, we must understand the mechanics of expiration in relation to lung volumes.

 

  • Expiratory force is greatest at Total Lung Capacity (TLC) because at maximum lung inflation, the muscles and elastic properties of the lung generate the highest pressure to forcefully exhale air.
  • As expiration progresses, the force gradually decreases until passive expiration takes over (e.g., at tidal volumes).
  • Beyond a certain point (closer to Residual Volume (RV)), expiratory effort becomes ineffective due to airway closure and increased resistance.

 

In the given graph:

 

  • Point B represents TLC (Total Lung Capacity), where expiratory effort is maximized because the lungs are fully inflated, and the expiratory muscles (rectus abdominis, transverse abdominis, and intercostal muscles) must work the hardest to expel air.

 

Thus, maximum expiratory force is generated at Point B, making option B the correct answer.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Point A: Likely represents tidal volume range, where expiration is mostly passive and does not require significant muscle effort.

 

Option C. Point C: Likely represents the end of normal expiration (Functional Residual Capacity, FRC), where passive elastic recoil contributes more than active expiratory muscle force.

 

Option D. Point D: This is closer to Residual Volume (RV), where expiratory muscles contribute minimally because the airways collapse due to dynamic compression, preventing further airflow out of the lungs.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Maximum expiratory force is generated at Total Lung Capacity (TLC), as this is the point where the expiratory muscles must work the hardest to expel air from fully inflated lungs.

questions.stem: All of the following are true about secretin except:

options.label: A
options.text: It is secreted by S cells of intestine

options.label: B
options.text: It causes release of alkaline pancreatic juice rich in enzymes

options.label: C
options.text: Its action is mediated via intracellular cAMP

questions.answerText: It causes release of alkaline pancreatic juice rich in enzymes
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) It causes release of alkaline pancreatic juice rich in enzymes 

 

Secretin is a hormone secreted by S cells in the duodenum in response to acidic chyme entering from the stomach. It plays a crucial role in regulating pH balance in the small intestine by stimulating the release of bicarbonate-rich pancreatic juice, which helps neutralize gastric acid.

 

  • Secretin does not stimulate the release of enzyme-rich pancreatic juice. Instead, it primarily induces bicarbonate secretion from pancreatic ductal cells, leading to an alkaline environment in the duodenum.
  • The release of digestive enzyme-rich pancreatic juice is mainly stimulated by cholecystokinin (CCK), not secretin.

 

Additionally, secretin exerts its effects through the cyclic AMP (cAMP) second messenger system, which facilitates bicarbonate secretion.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. It is secreted by S cells of the intestine: Secretin is produced by S cells in the duodenum in response to acidic chyme.

 

Option C. Its action is mediated via intracellular cAMP: Secretin works through the cAMP (cyclic AMP) second messenger system, which triggers bicarbonate release.

 

Option D. It neutralizes the gastric chyme: The bicarbonate secretion stimulated by secretin raises the pH of chyme, neutralizing stomach acid and protecting the duodenal mucosa.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Secretin is secreted by S cells of the duodenum and stimulates the pancreas to release bicarbonate-rich fluid to neutralize gastric acid. However, it does not promote enzyme-rich pancreatic secretion, which is the function of cholecystokinin (CCK).

questions.stem: A 55-year-old male presents with complaints of pain in epigastrium after meal and its relieved by vomiting, 2 kg weight loss. He has habit of taking 5-6 cups of tea in a day. Laboratory investigation shows total RBC count 4 millions/cumm, Hb 11.5 gm%. Which of the following is possible diagnosis:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Gastric Ulcer 

 

The patient presents with epigastric pain that worsens after eating and is relieved by vomiting, along with mild anemia. These symptoms are classic for a gastric ulcer rather than a duodenal ulcer or GERD.

 

Key Diagnostic Clues:

 

  1. Pain after meals → Suggests a gastric ulcer.
    • Gastric ulcers worsen when food is ingested because acid secretion increases and directly irritates the ulcerated gastric mucosa.
    • Duodenal ulcers, in contrast, cause pain 2–3 hours after eating when the stomach is empty.
  2. Relief after vomiting → Strongly supports gastric ulcer.
    • Vomiting helps expel gastric acid, temporarily relieving symptoms.
  3. Weight loss → Common in gastric ulcers.
    • The patient avoids eating to prevent pain, leading to weight loss.
    • Duodenal ulcers are often associated with weight gain because patients tend to eat more to relieve pain.
  4. Mild anemia (Hb: 11.5 g/dL, RBC: 4 million/cumm)
    • Chronic gastric ulcers may lead to slow gastrointestinal blood loss, contributing to anemia.
  5. Excessive tea consumption (5–6 cups daily)
    • Tea contains caffeine, which stimulates gastric acid secretion, potentially worsening gastric ulcers.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD):

 

  • GERD presents with burning chest pain (heartburn) and acid regurgitation, not pain relieved by vomiting.
  • GERD pain worsens in a recumbent position and is unrelated to meals.

 

Option C. Duodenal ulcer:

 

  • Pain occurs 2–3 hours after meals (not immediately after).
  • Symptoms improve with eating, unlike gastric ulcers.
  • Typically not associated with vomiting or weight loss.

 

Option D. Achalasia cardia:

 

  • Dysphagia (difficulty swallowing) is the hallmark symptom.
  • The patient does not have difficulty swallowing, making achalasia unlikely.
  • Classic barium swallow finding in achalasia = "Bird’s beak" appearance.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Gastric ulcers cause epigastric pain after eating, which is relieved by vomiting. In contrast, duodenal ulcers cause pain 2–3 hours after meals and improve with eating. Chronic gastric ulcers can lead to weight loss and mild anemia.
