questions.stem: In response to an increase in GFR, the proximal tubule and the loop of Henle demonstrate an increase in the rate of Na+ reabsorption. This phenomenon is called?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Glomerulo tubular balance

 

Glomerulotubular (GT) balance is a mechanism by which the proximal tubule and loop of Henle adjust sodium reabsorption in response to changes in glomerular filtration rate (GFR). This ensures that a constant fraction (~67%) of the filtered sodium and water is reabsorbed, preventing excessive sodium and fluid loss when GFR increases and avoiding sodium retention when GFR decreases.

 

  • When GFR increases, more sodium and water are filtered, and the proximal tubule compensates by increasing its reabsorption rate proportionally.
  • This process maintains sodium balance and prevents excessive fluid loss, independent of hormonal control.

 

The macula densa and tubuloglomerular feedback play a role in regulating GFR and sodium reabsorption by sensing sodium levels and adjusting tubule reabsorption accordingly.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Autoregulation:

 

  • Renal autoregulation refers to the kidney’s ability to maintain a constant GFR despite changes in blood pressure, primarily through afferent arteriole constriction or dilation. It does not specifically explain sodium reabsorption changes in response to GFR variations.

 

Option C. Mineralocorticoid escape:

 

  • Aldosterone escape (or mineralocorticoid escape) occurs in conditions of excess aldosterone, where the kidney prevents sodium retention by increasing sodium excretion via natriuresis.
  • It is unrelated to GFR-mediated changes in sodium reabsorption.

 

Option D. Saturation of tubular transport: 

 

  • Tubular transport mechanisms (like glucose and amino acid transporters) can become saturated when their reabsorptive capacity is exceeded (e.g., glucose in diabetes).
  • However, GT balance ensures that sodium reabsorption scales with GFR, preventing transporter saturation.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Glomerulotubular balance ensures that the proximal tubule and loop of Henle reabsorb a constant fraction of filtered sodium and water, preventing excessive loss when GFR increases.

questions.stem: Which one of the following clinical disorder specifically arises due to the defective functioning of aquaporins, notably AQP2, crucial for water reabsorption in the kidney tubules, which disrupts the kidney's ability to concentrate urine, resulting in a distinctive pattern of excessive urine output, thirst, and potential dehydration despite adequate fluid intake.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Nephrogenic DI

 

Nephrogenic Diabetes Insipidus (DI) is a disorder characterized by the inability of the kidneys to respond to Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH, also called vasopressin). The condition results from a defect in AQP2 (Aquaporin-2) water channels in the collecting ducts, leading to:

 

  • Excessive urine output (polyuria)
  • Excessive thirst (polydipsia)
  • Inability to concentrate urine, causing hypotonic urine and risk of dehydration

 

There are two major types of DI:

 

  1. Central DI – Due to a lack of ADH secretion from the hypothalamus.
  2. Nephrogenic DI – Due to a defect in AQP2 or ADH receptor (V2 receptor) in the kidneys, preventing proper water reabsorption in the collecting ducts.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Liddle Syndrome.

 

  • Liddle syndrome is a gain-of-function mutation in the ENaC (Epithelial Sodium Channel) in the collecting duct, leading to:
    • Hypertension (due to sodium retention)
    • Hypokalemia
    • Metabolic alkalosis
  • It does not involve AQP2 dysfunction and does not cause excessive urine output.

 

Option C. Von Hippel-Lindau Syndrome 

 

  • A genetic disorder caused by mutations in the VHL tumor suppressor gene, leading to:
    • Hemangioblastomas in the brain and retina
    • Renal cell carcinoma (RCC)
    • Renal cysts
  • It has no relation to AQP2 defects or nephrogenic DI.

 

Option D. Bartter Syndrome 

 

  • A disorder affecting ion transport in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, resulting in:
    • Hypokalemia
    • Metabolic alkalosis
    • Polyuria (due to salt-wasting nephropathy)
  • However, Bartter syndrome is not caused by AQP2 defects but by mutations in sodium, potassium, and chloride transporters (NKCC2, ROMK, and CLC-Kb).

 

Educational Objective:

 

Nephrogenic Diabetes Insipidus (DI) occurs due to defective AQP2 channels in the collecting ducts, leading to excessive urine output, dehydration, and polydipsia, as the kidney loses its ability to concentrate urine.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a measure of stroke volume?

options.label: A
options.text: Left ventricular end diastolic volume minus left ventricular end systolic volume

options.label: B
options.text: Ejection fraction times left ventricular end diastolic volume

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Ejection fraction times cardiac output 

 

Stroke volume (SV) is the volume of blood ejected from the left ventricle during each heartbeat. It can be determined using several formulas:

 

  • A. Stroke Volume = Left Ventricular End Diastolic Volume (LVEDV) - Left Ventricular End Systolic Volume (LVESV)
    This formula calculates how much blood is expelled during contraction, making it a correct measure of stroke volume.
  • B. Stroke Volume = Ejection Fraction × LVEDV
    Ejection fraction (EF) is defined as the fraction of the end-diastolic volume that is ejected with each beat. Since EF is calculated as SV/LVEDV, multiplying EF by LVEDV results in stroke volume.
  • D. Stroke Volume = Cardiac Output / Heart Rate
    Cardiac output (CO) is the total blood volume pumped per minute, and since CO = Stroke Volume × Heart Rate, rearranging gives SV = CO / HR.

 

The incorrect option is Ejection Fraction × Cardiac Output because there is no direct relationship between ejection fraction and cardiac output that defines stroke volume.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Stroke volume can be calculated using different formulas, primarily:

 

  1. LVEDV - LVESV
  2. Ejection Fraction × LVEDV
  3. Cardiac Output / Heart Rate

 

The incorrect formula, Ejection Fraction × Cardiac Output, should be recognized as not a valid measure of stroke volume.

questions.stemHtml: During starvation, graph of three substances are plotted as below. The scale for A and B is on the left and the scale for C is on the right. Which of the substances are represented by the curve B?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) T3 

 

During starvation, the body's metabolism adapts to conserve energy by altering thyroid hormone levels:

 

  1. T4 (Thyroxine) levels decrease slightly, but the reduction is not drastic. This is because T4 serves as a reservoir that can be converted into either T3 or reverse T3 (rT3).
  2. T3 (Triiodothyronine) levels decrease significantly. T3 is the active form of thyroid hormone responsible for increasing metabolism. Since the body aims to conserve energy, T3 production is reduced.
  3. Reverse T3 (rT3) levels increase. rT3 is an inactive form of T3. The body converts more T4 into rT3 instead of T3 during starvation to slow down metabolic rate and preserve energy.

 

From the graph:

 

  • Curve A represents rT3, which rises during starvation.
  • Curve B represents T3, which drops significantly to conserve energy.
  • Curve C represents T4, which shows a slight decline but remains relatively stable.

 

Thus, Curve B corresponds to T3, making option C the correct answer.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. RT3 - Reverse T3: Incorrect. RT3 increases during starvation, following the opposite trend of T3. This corresponds to Curve A in the graph.

 

Option B. T4 - Thyroxine: Incorrect. T4 levels do decrease slightly but not drastically. This corresponds to Curve C in the graph.

 

Option D. DIT - Diiodotyrosine: Incorrect. DIT is a precursor in thyroid hormone synthesis and is not directly measured in the context of starvation response.

 

Educational Objective:

 

During starvation, T3 levels drop significantly to reduce metabolic rate, rT3 levels increase to inhibit metabolism, and T4 levels show a mild decrease but remain relatively stable.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman undergoes total thyroidectomy for papillary thyroid cancer. Following, surgery the patient develops perioral numbness and spasm of the muscles of her hand. The latter change is due to a change in the resting membrane potential of cells. Which of the below mentioned conditions will have a similar effect on the RMP of a cell?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Conn’s syndrome 

 

The symptoms described—perioral numbness and muscle spasms—are indicative of hypocalcemia, a common postoperative complication of total thyroidectomy due to accidental removal or dysfunction of the parathyroid glands, which regulate calcium levels via parathyroid hormone (PTH).

 

Calcium plays a crucial role in stabilizing the resting membrane potential (RMP) by decreasing sodium permeability. When calcium levels drop, sodium influx increases, leading to hyperexcitability of nerves and muscles (as seen in tetany).

 

Conn’s syndrome (Primary Hyperaldosteronism) causes increased calcium excretion, leading to hypocalcemia, which in turn increases sodium permeability, making the membrane more excitable. This mimics the effects of post-thyroidectomy hypocalcemia.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. SIADH - Syndrome of Inappropriate ADH Secretion: Incorrect. SIADH causes hyponatremia, which can lead to neurological symptoms but does not significantly affect RMP in the same way hypocalcemia does.

 

Option C. Bolus Injection of Insulin: Incorrect. Insulin primarily shifts potassium into cells, temporarily reducing extracellular potassium, but it does not significantly affect calcium levels or RMP in the way hypocalcemia does.

 

Option D. Multiple Myeloma: Incorrect. Multiple myeloma can cause hypercalcemia, the opposite of what is seen in this patient. Increased calcium stabilizes the membrane, making it less excitable, which is not the effect described in this case.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Hypocalcemia lowers the resting membrane potential by increasing sodium permeability, leading to increased excitability and muscle spasms. Conditions like primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn’s syndrome) can increase calcium excretion, leading to hypocalcemia and similar neuromuscular symptoms.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old girl with a head injury from a car accident was brought to the emergency department by ambulance. On exam, she had a respiratory rate of 8 breaths per minute, and a prolonged duration of inhalation was noted. Damage to which of the following groups of neurons in the brainstem is most likely responsible for this abnormal respiration?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Pneumotaxic center 

 

The pneumotaxic center, located in the upper pons, regulates the rate and pattern of breathing by inhibiting inspiration and controlling the transition from inspiration to expiration. When the pneumotaxic center is damaged, this inhibition is lost, leading to prolonged inspiration and a decreased respiratory rate.

 

In this case, the patient has a slow respiratory rate (8 breaths per minute) and prolonged inhalation, which suggests that the pneumotaxic center is not functioning properly. With this inhibition removed, inspiratory neurons (in the medulla) are activated for a longer duration, causing deep and prolonged inspiration with a reduced rate.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Dorsal Respiratory Group - DRG: Incorrect. DRG, located in the medulla, controls basic rhythmic breathing by receiving sensory input and stimulating inspiratory muscles. Damage to DRG would cause irregular breathing patterns, not a prolonged inhalation with a reduced rate.

 

Option B. Nucleus Tractus Solitarius - NTS: Incorrect. NTS is involved in processing sensory input from the vagus and glossopharyngeal nerves, playing a role in chemoreceptor and baroreceptor reflexes. It does not directly regulate the timing of inspiration.

 

 

Option D. Vasomotor Center: Incorrect. The vasomotor center, located in the medulla, regulates blood pressure and cardiovascular function, not respiration. Damage to this center would cause blood pressure abnormalities, not changes in breathing patterns.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The pneumotaxic center in the pons controls respiratory rate by inhibiting prolonged inspiration. Damage to this center leads to prolonged inspiration and a reduced respiratory rate.

questions.stem: Many signalling pathways involve the generation of inositol trisphosphate (IP3) and diacylglycerol (DAG). These molecules:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Are derived from PIP2 

 

IP3 (Inositol trisphosphate) and DAG (Diacylglycerol) are secondary messengers generated from phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) through the action of phospholipase C (PLC).

 

  1. Signaling Pathway Overview:
    • A first messenger (such as a hormone like oxytocin, ADH, or adrenaline via α1 receptors) binds to a G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR).
    • This activates the Gq protein, which in turn activates phospholipase C (PLC).
    • PLC hydrolyzes PIP2 (a membrane phospholipid) into IP3 and DAG.
    • IP3 stimulates calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
    • DAG activates protein kinase C (PKC), leading to further downstream signaling.

 

Since IP3 and DAG are produced from PIP2, the correct answer is Option D.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Are first messengers: Incorrect. First messengers are extracellular hormones or neurotransmitters (e.g., oxytocin, ADH, epinephrine). IP3 and DAG are intracellular second messengers.

 

Option B. Activate phospholipase C: Incorrect. Phospholipase C is activated upstream by Gq-protein signaling. IP3 and DAG do not activate PLC; rather, they are the products of PLC activation.

 

Option C. Can activate tyrosine kinase receptors: Incorrect. Tyrosine kinase receptors (TKRs) are activated by ligands such as insulin or growth factors (e.g., EGF, IGF). IP3 and DAG function downstream of G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), not TKRs.

 

Educational Objective:

 

IP3 and DAG are second messengers derived from PIP2 via phospholipase C activation. IP3 facilitates calcium release, while DAG activates protein kinase C, both leading to intracellular signaling cascades.

questions.stem: What is the effect of sympathetic stimulation on GFR?

options.label: A
options.text: Increase in GFR with afferent arteriolar dilation

options.label: B
options.text: Increase in GFR with efferent arteriolar dilation

options.label: C
options.text: Decrease in GFR with afferent arteriolar constriction

options.label: D
options.text: Decrease in GFR with efferent arteriolar constriction

questions.answerText: Decrease in GFR with afferent arteriolar constriction
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Decrease in GFR with afferent arteriolar constriction

 

Sympathetic stimulation plays a crucial role in regulating renal blood flow and glomerular filtration rate (GFR), especially during stressful situations (e.g., hemorrhage, dehydration, exercise, shock).

 

  1. Sympathetic activation leads to vasoconstriction of both afferent and efferent arterioles, but afferent arteriolar constriction is more pronounced.
  2. Constriction of the afferent arteriole reduces renal blood flow (RBF), leading to a decrease in glomerular hydrostatic pressure, which subsequently decreases GFR.
  3. This helps conserve fluid and maintain blood pressure by reducing urine output.

 

Thus, the correct choice is "Decrease in GFR with afferent arteriolar constriction" (Option C).

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Increase in GFR with afferent arteriolar dilation: Incorrect. Sympathetic stimulation causes vasoconstriction, not dilation, especially in the afferent arteriole, leading to a decrease rather than an increase in GFR.

 

Option B. Increase in GFR with efferent arteriolar dilation: Incorrect. Dilation of the efferent arteriole would lead to decreased glomerular pressure and a reduced GFR, not an increase.

 

Option D. Decrease in GFR with efferent arteriolar constriction: Incorrect. Although sympathetic stimulation does cause some degree of efferent arteriolar constriction, it is less than the afferent constriction, and isolated efferent constriction would actually increase GFR, not decrease it.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Sympathetic stimulation decreases GFR by predominantly constricting the afferent arteriole, reducing renal blood flow and glomerular hydrostatic pressure. This mechanism helps conserve body fluids and maintain systemic blood pressure in stress conditions.

questions.stem: Which characteristic physiological response pattern is associated with a pulmonary reflex mechanism stimulated by the activation of pulmonary J-receptors, specifically related to the release of inflammatory mediators or pulmonary congestion in conditions such as pulmonary edema or interstitial lung disease?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Slow breathing, bradycardia, hypotension 

 

Pulmonary Juxtacapillary (J) receptors are mechanoreceptors located in the alveolar interstitium near pulmonary capillaries. These receptors are activated in conditions such as pulmonary edema, interstitial lung disease, and inflammation due to increased fluid or chemical irritation.

 

  1. Activation of J-receptors triggers the J-reflex (Bezold-Jarisch Reflex), which leads to:
    • Apnea or slowed breathing (hypopnea) or shallow breathing
    • Bradycardia (slow heart rate)
    • Hypotension (low blood pressure)
  2. The physiological mechanism is similar to the Bezold-Jarisch reflex in the heart, which is triggered by chemical stimuli like capsaicin, serotonin, and vanilloid substances.
  3. The reduction in respiratory rate, heart rate, and blood pressure is a protective response aimed at minimizing further fluid accumulation and stress on the pulmonary system.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Pulmonary J-receptor activation (J-reflex) occurs in conditions like pulmonary edema and interstitial lung disease, causing:

 

  • Slow breathing (hypopnea or shallow respiration)
  • Bradycardia (decreased heart rate)
  • Hypotension (decreased blood pressure)

 

This response is similar to the Bezold-Jarisch reflex, which is a protective reflex that reduces cardiorespiratory stress.

questions.stem: Which one of the following statement accurately describes the a neurological phenomenon commonly observed in motor control and pivotal in maintaining appropriate muscle tension, involves a specific neuronal pathway with interneuronal processing between sensory and motor neurons, regulating muscle contraction by modulating motor neuron activity based on Golgi tendon organ input."

options.label: A
options.text: Occurs when IA spindle afferents are inhibited.

options.label: B
options.text: Is a monosynaptic reflex initiated by activation of the Golgi tendon organ.

options.label: C
options.text: Is a disynaptic reflex with a single interneuron inserted between the afferent and efferent limbs.

options.label: D
options.text: Uses type II afferent fibers from the Golgi tendon organ

questions.answerText: Is a disynaptic reflex with a single interneuron inserted between the afferent and efferent limbs.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Is a disynaptic reflex with a single interneuron inserted between the afferent and efferent limbs. 

 

The Golgi tendon organ (GTO) reflex, also known as the inverse stretch reflex, is crucial for preventing excessive muscle tension and potential muscle damage.

 

  1. Mechanism of the Reflex:
    • The Golgi tendon organ (GTO), located at the musculotendinous junction, detects excessive muscle tension.
    • It is activated when muscle contraction generates high tension.
    • The GTO sends sensory input via group Ib afferent fibers to the spinal cord.
    • The Ib afferents synapse onto inhibitory interneurons in the spinal cord.
    • The inhibitory interneuron inhibits the alpha motor neuron, leading to muscle relaxation to prevent damage.
  2. Key Features of the Reflex:
    • It is a disynaptic reflex: A single inhibitory interneuron is present between the afferent (Ib fiber) and the efferent (alpha motor neuron).
    • It functions to relax the muscle under excessive tension, ensuring muscle protection from injury.

 

Thus, the correct answer is Option C: "Is a disynaptic reflex with a single interneuron inserted between the afferent and efferent limbs."

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Occurs when IA spindle afferents are inhibited: 

 

  • Ia afferents are involved in the muscle spindle stretch reflex, not the Golgi tendon reflex.
  • Muscle spindles sense muscle length, whereas GTOs sense muscle tension.
  • The GTO reflex does not inhibit Ia afferents; it inhibits the alpha motor neurons to reduce muscle contraction.

 

Option B. Is a monosynaptic reflex initiated by activation of the Golgi tendon organ: 

 

  • Monosynaptic reflexes, like the stretch reflex, involve only one synapse (e.g., knee jerk reflex).
  • The GTO reflex requires an inhibitory interneuron, making it disynaptic, not monosynaptic.

 

Option D. Uses type II afferent fibers from the Golgi tendon organ:

 

  • Type II afferents are associated with the muscle spindle and detect static muscle length.
  • The Golgi tendon organ uses group Ib afferent fibers, not type II fibers.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The Golgi tendon reflex is a disynaptic inhibitory reflex that:

 

  • Prevents excessive muscle tension to protect the muscle from damage.
  • Uses group Ib afferent fibers from the Golgi tendon organ.
  • Inhibits the alpha motor neuron via an inhibitory interneuron, leading to muscle relaxation.

questions.stemHtml: What waves are shown as X & Y below:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Alpha and delta

 

The graph shows two different waveforms labeled as X and Y, which correspond to different brain wave frequencies. Brain waves are classified based on their frequency range:

 

Step-by-step Analysis:

 

  1. Counting the waves per second:
    • X (Red waveform): Shows 9-10 waves per second, which falls within the Alpha wave range (8-13 Hz).
    • Y (Green waveform): Shows 1-2 waves per second, indicating a low-frequency wave, which matches the Delta wave range (<4 Hz).
  2. Matching the frequency with wave type:
    • The red waveform (X) represents Alpha waves (8–13 Hz), commonly seen in a relaxed awake state.
    • The green waveform (Y) represents Delta waves (<4 Hz), typically observed in deep sleep stages (NREM3).

 

Thus, Option B (Alpha and Delta waves) is the correct answer.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Alpha and Theta waves: Incorrect. The lower frequency waveform (Y) is too slow to be a theta wave (4-7 Hz). It is more consistent with Delta waves.

 

Option C. Beta and Theta waves: Incorrect. X is not a Beta wave, as it has fewer than 14 Hz. Additionally, Y is too slow to be a Theta wave.

 

Option D. Beta and Delta waves: Incorrect. X is an Alpha wave, not a Beta wave. Delta waves are present, but Beta waves are not.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Alpha waves (8-13 Hz) appear during relaxed, wakeful states.
  • Delta waves (<4 Hz) are dominant during deep sleep (NREM3).
  • Brain waves can be identified by counting the frequency (waves per second) to classify them correctly.

questions.stem: A 13-year-old male is brought to the clinic by his parents with complains of facial puffiness and increased weight gain in past 1 week. Urine examination showed massive proteinuria and traces of blood. Which of the following pressures favors glomerular filtration?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Glomerular capillary pressure 

 

Glomerular filtration is determined by the Starling forces, which include hydrostatic and oncotic pressures within the glomerular capillaries and Bowman’s space. These pressures either favor or oppose filtration.

 

Glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure (PGC) (Favors Filtration) 

 

  • This is the main driving force for glomerular filtration.
  • It pushes plasma out of the glomerular capillaries into Bowman’s space, facilitating filtration.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Glomerular capillary oncotic pressure: 

 

  • This pressure is generated by plasma proteins (e.g., albumin) that retain fluid inside capillaries and oppose filtration.
  • In nephrotic syndrome (suggested by massive proteinuria and facial puffiness), plasma oncotic pressure decreases, favoring filtration, but in normal physiology, it acts as a resisting force.

 

Option C. Bowman’s space hydrostatic pressure: (Opposes Filtration):

 

  • This pressure is due to fluid present in Bowman’s space.
  • If this pressure is increased (e.g., urinary obstruction or kidney stones), it opposes filtration by pushing fluid back into capillaries.

 

Option D. All of the above: Incorrect. Only glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure favors filtration, while the other two oppose it.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Glomerular filtration is primarily driven by glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure (PGC), which promotes filtration. Opposing forces include glomerular oncotic pressure and Bowman’s space hydrostatic pressure, which resist filtration.

questions.stem: Through what “permissive action” do glucocorticoids accelerate gluconeogenesis during fasting?

options.label: A
options.text: Glucocorticoids stimulate the secretion of insulin, which activates gluconeogenic enzymes in the liver

options.label: B
options.text: Glucocorticoids inhibit the use of glucose by skeletal muscle

options.label: C
options.text: Glucocorticoids maintain the vascular response to norepinephrine

options.label: D
options.text: Glucocorticoids maintain the intracellular concentrations of many of the enzymes needed to carry out gluconeogenesis through effects on transcription

questions.answerText: Glucocorticoids maintain the intracellular concentrations of many of the enzymes needed to carry out gluconeogenesis through effects on transcription
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Glucocorticoids maintain the intracellular concentrations of many of the enzymes needed to carry out gluconeogenesis through effects on transcription 

 

Glucocorticoids, particularly cortisol, play a crucial role in maintaining blood glucose levels during fasting by exerting a permissive effect on metabolic processes. They do not directly stimulate gluconeogenesis but rather increase the transcription of enzymes required for gluconeogenesis, ensuring that the body can effectively generate glucose when needed.

 

Key Mechanism of Glucocorticoid Action in Gluconeogenesis:

 

  1. Transcriptional Regulation:
    • Glucocorticoids enter cells and bind to intracellular glucocorticoid receptors, which then act on glucocorticoid response elements (GREs) in the DNA to upregulate gluconeogenic enzymes.
    • Key gluconeogenic enzymes induced by glucocorticoids include:
      • Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PEPCK)
      • Glucose-6-phosphatase (G6Pase)
      • Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase
    • This ensures that the body can generate glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors (e.g., amino acids, lactate) when fasting.
  2. Prepares the Liver for Gluconeogenesis:
    • Glucocorticoids do not directly initiate gluconeogenesis but prime the liver by ensuring the availability of necessary enzymes so that, when signals like glucagon or epinephrine activate gluconeogenesis, the process is efficient.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Glucocorticoids stimulate the secretion of insulin, which activates gluconeogenic enzymes in the liver: 

 

  • Insulin inhibits gluconeogenesis, not promotes it.
  • Insulin stimulates glycolysis (glucose utilization), not gluconeogenesis (glucose production).

 

Option B. Glucocorticoids inhibit the use of glucose by skeletal muscle: 

 

  • While glucocorticoids promote protein catabolism in skeletal muscle to provide amino acids for gluconeogenesis, they do not inhibit glucose uptake in skeletal muscle.
  • In contrast, insulin resistance in chronic glucocorticoid excess (Cushing’s syndrome) can lead to reduced glucose uptake, but that is not their direct mechanism of action during fasting.

 

Option C. Glucocorticoids maintain the vascular response to norepinephrine: 

 

  • While glucocorticoids do play a role in maintaining vascular tone and blood pressure by upregulating adrenergic receptors, this has nothing to do with gluconeogenesis.
  • The question asks specifically about gluconeogenesis, making this an irrelevant choice.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Glucocorticoids do not directly trigger gluconeogenesis but exert a permissive effect by increasing the transcription of key gluconeogenic enzymes. This ensures that when fasting conditions arise, the body has the necessary molecular machinery to generate glucose from non-carbohydrate sources to maintain blood glucose levels.

questions.stem: A 3yrs old boy comes to your clinic with puffy eyes, generalised oedema all over the body. Urine output is low. Proteinuria, No blood in urine. What is the cause of oedema?

options.label: A
options.text: Built up of body fluids outside tissue.

options.label: B
options.text: The increase in fluid is related to decrease leak from the blood.

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Reduced removal by lymph system

 

This 3-year-old boy presents with generalized edema and proteinuria, which is highly suggestive of nephrotic syndrome (likely minimal change disease, the most common cause in children).

 

Edema in nephrotic syndrome:

 

  1. Loss of plasma proteins (hypoalbuminemia) → Causes decreased plasma oncotic pressure.
  2. Reduced oncotic pressure → Leads to fluid leaking out from capillaries into the interstitial space, causing edema.
  3. Lymphatic drainage normally helps remove excess interstitial fluid → But in severe hypoalbuminemia, the lymphatic system cannot compensate, leading to persistent edema.

 

Since the lymphatic system plays a crucial role in returning interstitial fluid to circulation, when its function is overwhelmed due to persistent low oncotic pressure, edema worsens.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Build-up of body fluids outside tissue: While edema does involve fluid accumulation in the interstitium, this option is too vague and does not explain the mechanism of edema in nephrotic syndrome.

 

Option B. The increase in fluid is related to decreased leak from the blood: The opposite is true—proteinuria causes a reduction in plasma oncotic pressure, which increases capillary leak, leading to more fluid loss into the interstitial space.

 

Option D. Thyroid is responsible for edema: Hypothyroidism can cause myxedema (non-pitting edema), but there is no history of thyroid dysfunction in this child, and nephrotic syndrome is a much more likely cause of his symptoms.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Nephrotic syndrome leads to hypoalbuminemia, causing decreased plasma oncotic pressure and increased interstitial fluid leakage. The lymphatic system initially compensates but eventually gets overwhelmed, leading to persistent edema.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man was brought to the emergency with confusion and lethargy. His temperature is 36.7 C, blood pressure is 86/58 mmHg, pulse is 120/min, and respirations are 10/min. pH is 7.59, pCO2 49 mmHg and P02 of 85mm Hg. Which of the following condition best describe his acid base status?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Metabolic alkalosis

 

To determine the acid-base disorder, follow these steps:

 

  1. Step 1: Evaluate pH
    • Normal pH range: 7.35 - 7.45
    • Patient’s pH: 7.59 (Elevated) → Alkalosis is present
  2. Step 2: Determine the primary disorder
    • If the disorder is respiratory, the pCO2 (carbon dioxide) should move in the opposite direction of pH.
    • If the disorder is metabolic, the HCO3- (bicarbonate) should move in the same direction as pH.
    • Patient’s pCO2: 49 mmHg (Elevated)
      • Normally, pCO2 is around 40 mmHg.
      • If this were respiratory alkalosis, we would expect low pCO2 (since hyperventilation "blows off" CO2).
      • However, here, pCO2 is high, which suggests the body is trying to compensate for an alkalotic condition rather than causing it.
      • This means the primary issue is metabolic.
  3. Step 3: Confirm metabolic alkalosis
    • In metabolic alkalosis, the pH is high, and bicarbonate levels increase.
    • The kidneys retain bicarbonate, leading to alkalosis.
    • The body compensates via hypoventilation (slow breathing) to retain CO2, which explains why pCO2 is elevated in this case.

 

Thus, the primary disturbance is metabolic alkalosis with respiratory compensation.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Respiratory alkalosis:

 

  • In respiratory alkalosis, pCO2 would be low, not high.
  • The patient’s pCO2 is elevated, ruling out this option.

 

Option B. Respiratory acidosis:

 

  • Respiratory acidosis occurs when pH is low (<7.35) with elevated pCO2, usually due to hypoventilation (e.g., COPD, drug overdose).
  • Here, pH is high (alkalosis), ruling out acidosis.

 

Option D. Metabolic acidosis:

 

  • Metabolic acidosis presents with low pH (<7.35) and low bicarbonate (HCO3-).
  • Here, pH is high, meaning this is not acidosis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Metabolic alkalosis occurs when pH is high due to excess bicarbonate retention or acid loss (e.g., vomiting, diuretics, hyperaldosteronism).
  • Compensation occurs via respiratory hypoventilation, leading to increased pCO2, as seen in this patient.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old female presents with primary amenorrhea, weight gain, loss of appetite, cold intolerance. She also complains of anosmia. On further investigations, a diagnosis of Kallman's syndrome is made. Which of the following statements regarding olfactory pathway is incorrect?

options.label: A
options.text: Cilia of olfactory cells extends into the mucosal layer

options.label: B
options.text: Mitral cells are second order neurons

options.label: C
options.text: Mucus is produced by supporting cells and Bowman's gland

options.label: D
options.text: Olfactory cortex is present on medial parietal lobe

questions.answerText: Olfactory cortex is present on medial parietal lobe
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Olfactory cortex is present on medial parietal lobe. 

 

Kallmann’s syndrome is characterized by hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and anosmia (loss of smell) due to failure of migration of GnRH neurons and olfactory neurons during fetal development.

 

  • The olfactory cortex is NOT located in the medial parietal lobe.
  • Instead, it is primarily in the medial temporal lobe, particularly the piriform cortex, amygdala, and parts of the orbitofrontal cortex.
  • Unlike other sensory modalities, olfactory signals bypass the thalamus and reach the cortex directly. (Incorrect statement → Option D is false, making it the correct answer).

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Cilia of olfactory cells extend into the mucosal layer: Olfactory receptor neurons have cilia that extend into the mucus, allowing odorant molecules to bind to receptors.

 

Option B. Mitral cells are second-order neurons: Mitral and tufted cells in the olfactory bulb are second-order neurons, relaying sensory information to the brain.

 

Option C. Mucus is produced by supporting cells and Bowman's gland: Mucus is secreted by supporting cells and Bowman’s glands to dissolve odorants and facilitate detection by olfactory receptors.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The olfactory pathway involves:

 

  1. Olfactory receptors (bipolar neurons) in the nasal epithelium detecting odorants.
  2. Mitral and tufted cells (second-order neurons) in the olfactory bulb relaying signals.
  3. Olfactory cortex (medial temporal lobe, NOT parietal lobe) processing olfactory information.
  4. Bypassing the thalamus, making olfaction unique among sensory pathways.

 

Olfactory cortex is present on medial temporal lobe
